common_name: Gallery Series Lupine (Compact Mixed-Color Dwarf Strain)

planting.note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Gallery is a compact strain needing little to no staking.

directions: Gallery is a compact, uniform strain of garden lupine bred to bring the full spectrum of Russell-type flower colors to a shorter, front-of-border scale, with named color forms such as Gallery Red, Gallery Blue, Gallery Yellow, and Gallery Pink sold both individually and as a mixed blend. Because plants stay well under two feet tall, the dense flower spikes rarely need staking even in exposed sites, making the strain a popular choice for patio containers and small cottage gardens. As with other lupines, seedlings resent root disturbance, so start Gallery types where they are to grow or transplant only while very young. The strain shares the cool-summer preference of its Russell-type parentage and tends to struggle through hot, humid summers.

planting.note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil.

directions: My Castle is one of the oldest named selections from the classic Russell strain of garden lupine, valued for its rich brick-red to crimson flower spikes that stand out among the more common blues and purples of seed-grown mixes. Like the related The Governor and The Chatelaine selections, it has remained in cultivation for decades as a favorite of gardeners wanting a consistent, true-breeding color rather than a mixed strain. Tall, dense spires of pea-like flowers rise above handsome palmately compound foliage in early summer, attracting bumblebees and other pollinators. The plant performs best in cool climates with moist, well-drained soil and typically declines in regions with hot, humid summers.

common_name: Blue Bird Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Blue Bird is one of the original University of Saskatchewan haskap releases and needs a compatible pollinizer cultivar with overlapping bloom time planted nearby.

directions: Blue Bird was part of the founding quartet of University of Saskatchewan haskap releases, alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Moon, selected from the same early breeding population for its rounder, more compact berries and dependable, heavy fruit set. Like its siblings it flowers very early in spring and is self-infertile, so plant it with a compatible cultivar that blooms at the same time to ensure a full crop. The fruit carries the classic sweet-tart, blueberry-raspberry flavor of early-generation haskaps, though later University of Saskatchewan introductions have since surpassed it in fruit size and flavor, leaving Blue Bird grown today mostly in heritage collections and as a pollen source for its still-popular siblings. Give it the same well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun as other haskaps, and limit pruning to dead or crossing wood for the first several years while the shrub's framework establishes.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

common_name: Mountain Pride Tomato (Early North Carolina State Disease-Resistant Determinate)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Pride is a compact determinate hybrid suited to staking or caging rather than a full trellis.

directions: Mountain Pride was released by North Carolina State University's vegetable breeding program in 1979 as one of the earliest entries in what became the Mountain series, bred as a determinate hybrid carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt and Fusarium wilt for more reliable production in the humid Southern Appalachians. Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after frost danger passes, staking or caging the relatively compact plants to keep the developing fruit off the ground. It sets a concentrated main crop of firm, medium-large red globes with good old-fashioned tomato flavor over a shorter harvest window than later Mountain-series introductions bred for extended production. Though largely superseded in modern trials by Mountain Spring and its descendants, Mountain Pride is still offered by a few heirloom-minded seed companies for gardeners wanting the original Mountain-series disease package.
sources: North Carolina State University Mountain Horticultural Crops Research and Extension Center
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

common_name: Mountain Spring Tomato (North Carolina State Disease-Resistant Determinate Slicer)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Spring is a sturdy determinate hybrid that benefits from staking or caging to support its heavy fruit load.

directions: Mountain Spring followed Mountain Pride out of the North Carolina State University breeding program, released in 1991 with broader disease resistance and a heavier, more concentrated fruit set that made it a standard commercial and home-garden slicer across the Southeast through the 1990s. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun, staking the sturdy determinate plants to carry the crop of large, firm red globes. It carries resistance to Verticillium wilt and multiple races of Fusarium wilt along with useful field tolerance to early blight, a combination that kept foliage productive later into the season than older Southern-bred tomatoes of its era. Mountain Spring was eventually followed by newer Mountain-series releases such as Mountain Fresh and Mountain Merit, but it remains a dependable, widely adapted choice for home gardens across USDA zones 6-9.
sources: North Carolina State University Mountain Horticultural Crops Research and Extension Center
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; mulch heavily over winter in the coldest parts of its range.

directions: Micmac is an early-to-mid-season strawberry released by the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia, valued through the mid-20th century for outstanding winter hardiness and reliable cropping in the short-season, cold-winter regions of Atlantic Canada. Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and mulch the planting heavily over winter in the coldest parts of its range. The berries run small to medium with firm flesh well suited to preserves, and plants throw vigorous runners that fill in a matted row quickly. Though long superseded by later Kentville and Ottawa introductions for fresh-market use, Micmac's hardiness made it valuable breeding stock, contributing to later cold-tolerant cultivars such as Glooscap.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants to give the vigorous runners room to fill in a matted row.

directions: Bounty was bred at Agriculture Canada's Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa and released for its vigorous, heavy-yielding plants and good general disease tolerance, making it a dependable mid-season strawberry for the cooler strawberry-growing regions of Canada and the northern United States. Plant bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, giving the vigorous runners plenty of room to fill in a matted row over the first season. Its firm, bright red berries hold up well for local sale and home preserving, though flavor is considered solid rather than exceptional next to modern dessert-type cultivars. Bounty's vigor and hardiness made it valuable parent stock for later Canadian strawberry breeding, including the widely grown cold-hardy cultivar Glooscap.
